claims.claim: Security fix authored, merged, then superseded into google/go-github
claims.detail: I authored #4556, which was merged by maintainer gmlewis on 2026-09-17: an upload whose URL pointed at a different host than the configured upload host was refused rather than sent with the client's credentials. He reverted it the next day in favour of his broader #4564, which now enforces the general rule in master ('credentials are sent only to configured origins', via AllowedOrigins in github/github.go) and which says verbatim in its own description: 'generalizing what #4556 did in one (thanks @sushant-me)'. #4564 also carries a merged commit titled 'Address feedback from sushant-me' - I reviewed the replacement and my feedback was adopted. He stated publicly on #4366 that he would carry the fixes and credit @sushant-me as a co-author; that credit has NOT yet landed, so it is not claimed. The superseded PR and its replacement are both linked, because 'merged' alone would describe code that is no longer in master.

claims.claim: The paper's committed artifacts reproduce from its committed sources
claims.detail: The repository ships the 600-scenario corpus, the raw model outputs for every condition, and the analysis, plus its own checker (src/verify_reproducibility.py, run by `make verify`). It passes on a fresh clone with no model execution: data/corpus.jsonl regenerates byte-for-byte from the generator, results/metrics.json reproduces from the raw outputs across 5 conditions, and 100 macros derive from metrics.json with any recorded constant declared as such. The numbers quoted elsewhere on my pages come from those artifacts - e.g. unsafe-accept rates 17.2% / 46.2% / 23.5%, decision accuracy 66.3%, and 6 of 208 hard denials approved in the best arm, where 208 is the count of Rule A scenarios in the committed corpus.
metrics: metrics reproduce from raw outputs, 5 conditions

claims.claim: tool-boundary-corpus - a labelled corpus of agent tool-boundary cases and a detector-agnostic harness that scores precision and recall
claims.detail: 18 cases (13 tool-list declarations, 5 framework-code) with positives citing where each pattern came from in the real world and negatives that are the correct implementation of the same job. Detectors are commands that print JSON, so any scanner can be scored. Measured: mcpaudit P=1.000 R=1.000 on tool-list; agentbound P=1.000 R=1.000 on code, up from 0.750 when the corpus found a false positive it reported (a pattern inside a string bound to a name) — agentbound v0.1.10 fixed it and the same harness re-measured the improvement. The harness is itself tested with fake detectors (perfect, silent, trigger-happy, crashing, malformed JSON), and the corpus is self-authored, which every report states.
metrics: found a real false positive that was then fixed

claims.claim: mcpaudit - review an MCP server's tool declarations before connecting, and pin them so a later change is visible
claims.detail: Static audit of a tools/list payload: reserved-name collisions (critical), instruction-shaped text, invisible Unicode with the tag-block payload decoded, look-alike tool names, destructive tools declaring readOnlyHint, unconstrained sink parameters. Silent on a well-behaved server, which is a test. A lock file with per-field hashes reports drift, including a changed description. It can also emit a starting policygate policy from the same declarations (deny/escalate/allow mapped from severity), which the integration tests load with the real policygate loader in CI. Writing the generator exposed a supply-chain bug in it: the tool name is attacker-controlled text written into the policy, and unescaped it could inject its own allow rule; every interpolated value is escaped now, with four regression tests.

claims.claim: policygate - a fail-closed policy gate for agent tool calls, built so a language model can never authorise an action
claims.detail: Rules are evaluated by severity rather than file order; ALLOW is produced only by an allow rule; a model may deny or escalate but its ALLOW on an uncovered call is overruled and recorded; a failing or unparseable evaluator falls through to the refusing default; every decision goes to a hash-chained audit log. Adapters wrap MCP-style servers, LangChain-style tools and provider-shaped function calls, duck-typed so no framework becomes a dependency. Verified by mutation: disabling the model-allow invariant fails three tests, disabling the unparseable-call path fails three, and disabling both fails six.

claims.claim: agentbound - static detector for AI-agent tool-boundary bugs
claims.detail: Five rules across Python, TypeScript and YAML for tool shadowing, reserved-name collisions, last-wins tool dictionaries and fail-open confirmation gates; each rule grounded in a real finding. v0.1.11 is the current release and fixes a release that reported the wrong version: v0.1.10 shipped with `__version__` still at 0.1.9, so the tag, the release name and `agentbound --version` disagreed, and a test now compares the two version strings. The false positive that v0.1.10 fixed was found by sushant-me/tool-boundary-corpus: a string bound to a name is prose, not code.
